tier_reason: Public harness tools/encoderbenchcmp/main.go, tools/csrc/libopus_encoder_bench.c, tools/testvectorbenchcmp/main.go and internal/libopustooling/libopustooling.go build libopus 1.6.1 with --enable-rtcd --enable-intrinsics and CFLAGS -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=x86-64-v3 -mtune=generic, and match application, bandwidth, frame size, bitrate, CBR, signal and complexity 10 on both sides; README and reports/validation.md state Go 1.27.1, GCC 13.3.0, GOAMD64=v3, PGO, AMD EPYC 7763 and revision 4b660d668, with a public Actions run (36852328909) holding the raw samples.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.1, GOAMD64=v3, GOEXPERIMENT=simd, -pgo=default.pgo (profile generated from the repo's own encode/decode benchmarks); libopus 1.6.1 static archive configured --enable-static --disable-shared --enable-rtcd --enable-intrinsics with CFLAGS -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=x86-64-v3 -mtune=generic (GCC 13.3.0; AVX2/FMA RTCD lane, opus_select_arch=4), C helper compiled -O3 -DNDEBUG with the same target, no PGO or LTO on the C side; scalar lanes use --disable-asm --disable-rtcd --disable-intrinsics plus -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-tree-slp-vectorize against Go -tags nosimd. The C side runs as a separate helper process timed internally with clock_gettime, so process start-up is excluded. Three runs of at least 250 ms per case, median reported. Reproduce with tools/encoderbenchcmp and tools/testvectorbenchcmp.
corrections.workload: Matched C and Go encode and decode workloads in ns per sample per channel. Encode (opus_encode_float vs gopus Encode, float32 PCM from deterministic synthetic signals, complexity 10, CBR, encoder reset per pass): CELT restricted-celt fullband 20 ms stereo 128 kbps, CELT 5 ms mono 64 kbps, SILK restricted-silk wideband 20 ms mono 32 kbps, Hybrid (application audio, voice signal) fullband 20 ms mono 64 kbps and stereo 96 kbps. Decode: RFC test vectors 01-12, 20,075 packets, as float32 and int16.
corrections.caveats: Mixed result, not a uniform win: Go SIMD is faster than matched libopus SIMD in four of five encoder cases (2.5-28.7% less time) but 14.6% slower in the 5 ms CELT case, and decode wins are small (7.7% float32, 3.1% int16); Go scalar is slower than C scalar in 6 of 7 rows (10.6-23.4% more time, only SILK encode 2.8% faster). The Go side is built with PGO from a profile trained on the repo's own encode/decode benchmarks while the C side has no PGO or LTO. Measured on a GitHub Actions EPYC 7763 runner (shared cloud VM) with three runs per case, so the 2.5-7.7% margins are close to run-to-run noise. The timed decode loop checks only decoded sample counts; parity with libopus is enforced by separate test suites (exact final range and exact PCM on recorded configurations, with narrow documented floating-point allowances), so float decode output is not claimed bit-exact everywhere. The table is for revision 4b660d668 (2026-10-01); later master commits (#519 'Use safer codec kernels', #523 'Use checked kernel views') changed kernels without a fresh AMD64 table (ARM64-only deltas within about 3% are recorded). The file-based bench-encode/bench-decode examples include opus_demo start-up and file I/O and are only rough. First-party harness, though fully public. The fork hujm2023/gopus (0 stars) shows older CI numbers where Go is 1.3-1.7x slower than libopus; those were not used.

notes: Harness checked line by line: controls match on both arms (complexity 10, CBR, same bitrate/bandwidth/signal/application/frame size) and libopus is a real intrinsics+RTCD build at the same x86-64-v3 target, so tier A holds; the entry is a mixed result with small margins and a PGO asymmetry, stated in caveats. The pure-Go claim is also its usability point: BSD-3-Clause, 27 stars, last commit 2026-10-02.

tier_reason: benchmarks/noasm-2026-09-08/README.md gives Rust 1.98.1 (LLVM 22.1.8), release/fat LTO/one codegen unit/RUSTFLAGS -C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=4, AMD Ryzen 9 7900X, pinned commits, and the public harness benchmarks/noasm-2026-09-08/reproduce.py with benchmarks/stills-2026-09-07/compare.py and benchmarks/upstream-2026-09-07/driver/src/main.rs (MD5-validated against upstream and dav1d 1.5.3); all numbers in the record appear there, but the A applies only to the no-assembly upstream baseline.

corrections.baseline: upstream memorysafety/rav1d commit d3d1cd6 (package 1.1.0) built with default-features=false (bitdepth_8, bitdepth_16 only), i.e. with its hand-written assembly disabled; not dav1d and not rav1d's default assembly build, both of which are faster
corrections.claimed_speedup: Against upstream rav1d without assembly only: checked rav1d-safe takes 0.680x the time with 1 worker (32.0% less decode time), 0.821x with 4 workers and 0.813x with 8 workers (geometric mean of 12 still inputs); for example photo-8k-min 1 worker 231.372 ms vs 451.903 ms (0.512x), while map inputs are 0.755-1.002x. Against assembly-enabled upstream rav1d it is slower: a separate 2026-09-07 page (different inputs: a 720x300 24-frame video, a 1024x1024 still, a 256x256 10-bit still; older rav1d-safe revision d1767a1) shows checked rav1d-safe taking 1.77-8.62 times as long with one frame in flight and up to 12.8x against upstream frame threading, and the README's historical v0.5.6 table shows 1.56x (4K) and 1.54x (8K) the ASM build's time on AVIF stills.
corrections.license: AGPL-3.0-only OR LicenseRef-Imazen-Commercial (Cargo.toml, LICENSE-AGPL3, LICENSE-COMMERCIAL); code inherited from dav1d/rav1d is BSD-2-Clause (COPYING)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 9 stars, 3 forks, 1,460 commits; crates.io rav1d-safe 0.6.0 published 2026-09-08, 15,003 total downloads
corrections.caveats: Not faster than the incumbent: against dav1d or assembly-enabled rav1d it is 1.5-8.6x slower on the author's own pages (1.54-1.56x on 4K/8K AVIF stills at v0.5.6; 1.77-8.62x on the 2026-09-07 video/still grid, up to 12.8x against upstream frame threading, which the checked fork cannot use yet). The only win is against upstream rav1d with its assembly turned off (which still contains unsafe Rust), on a 12-input still-image seed corpus (photo and map at 2K/4K/8K, minimum and eight tiles); map cells are near parity (0.755-1.002x) and the page says this is not a SIMD ablation and does not establish parity with the assembly default. Fixed A/B arm order may bias results. The 1.8-8.6x figures come from a separate page with different inputs and an older rav1d-safe revision, not the same page set. Dual AGPL-3.0/commercial licensing (copyleft; commercial key required for closed-source use) limits reuse. The baseline is not in the FFmpeg, x264, Opus list.

notes: Tier A stands for the no-assembly comparison (public reproduce.py, compiler, flags, CPU, MD5 checks). Usability left as mixed: the licences are OSI (AGPL-3.0-only, BSD-2-Clause for inherited code) but copyleft/commercial dual licensing plus a win only against a non-default upstream build make it a memory-safety pick, not a speed pick. Fixed 'same page set' wording, crate status (0.6.0 is published, not staged) and licence string.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark/README.md with public scripts (benchmark/run_audioflux.py, run_librosa.py, run_torchaudio.py, run_benchmark.py, utils.py) and CPU models, but no compiler, flags or BLAS build of the audioFlux C core is stated, so not A; the >50x librosa ratio also caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux AMD Threadripper 3970X: audioFlux 0.04294 s vs librosa 2.41958 s at 1 time step (about 56x, derived from page data) and 4.90343 s vs 51.62876 s at 3000 (about 10.5x, derived from page data); vs torchaudio 0.07707 s at 1 step and 5.86299 s at 3000, but torchaudio is faster at 100 steps (0.61876 s vs 0.67030 s). On Linux Intel i7-6850K audioFlux is slower than torchaudio at 10 steps and above (13.07378 s vs 12.14323 s at 3000); on macOS Intel and Apple M1 torchaudio is faster for short inputs (1-10 steps on macOS Intel, 5-100 steps on M1) while audioFlux is faster for long inputs (7.92596 s vs 24.84823 s at 3000 on macOS Intel).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 3.4k stars, 150 forks, 168 commits; PyPI audioflux 0.1.9 (2024-05-24), also on Anaconda
corrections.caveats: Off-baseline: compared only against Python libraries (librosa, torchaudio), not against a C/C++ codec or DSP baseline from the FFmpeg, x264, Opus list; essentia is listed but has no numbers. First-party benchmark on 2022-2023 versions (audioFlux 0.1.5, librosa 0.10.0, torchaudio 0.11.0); compiler, flags, BLAS backend and thread counts are not stated, and torchaudio/MKL threading is not controlled. Inputs are random noise (np.random.randn) timed with time.time() around one call, summed over 1000 runs. Settings are close but not identical: audioFlux uses Slaney mel scale with no filter normalisation, librosa defaults to Slaney normalisation, torchaudio uses its default HTK mel scale; outputs are not compared. torchaudio is faster than audioFlux on Linux Intel at 10 steps and above and on macOS for short inputs. The README also shows the results as chart images.

notes: Numbers match benchmark/README.md exactly; scripts are public and roughly matched (n_fft 2048, hop 512, 128 mels, center=False). Kept as off-baseline C entry per batch note; last commit 2026-03-06 (TuneTrack fixes), MIT.
